newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Feb 19.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Feb 19.

text.p: THE DOMINION

More allegations about misuse of public funds were raised under parliamentary privilege on Tuesday as opposition parties launched a vigorous attack on the government over the Aotearoa Television Network saga. Government ministers responded by defying opposition MPs to back up claims they dismissed as wild rumours unsubstantiated by fact. Opening an unruly snap debate on the ATN affair as parliament resumed after a nine-week break, Labour leader Helen Clark said it was "a sorry tale of ministerial incompetence, corporate greed, cronyism on the part of NZ First Ministers and grovelling by the majority partner in the Coalition to appease its junior partner". Page 1.

No full investigation was held into Winebox documents, Serious Fraud Office director Charles Sturt told the Cook Islands tax commission of inquiry on Tuesday. Sturt made the comment during questioning by Colin Carruthers, QC, about the accuracy of a press statement issued by Sturt in March 1994. He was also questioned about a statement to Attorney-General Paul East, in response to a question from Winston Peters in June 1994, which was not correct. Page 1.

The government had agreed to pay $2.675 million to the families of those affected by the 1995 Cave Creek tragedy, when 14 people died after a viewing platform collapsed in a national park, Attorney-General Paul East announced on Tuesday night. The compensation award was decided by mediator-arbitrator Sir Duncan McMullin, a former privy councillor and Conservation Authority chairman. East said the government would move promptly to implement the settlement. Page 2.

Spending $89 of Aotearoa Television's money on a pair of boxer shorts by NZ First MP Tukoroirangi Morgan could not be justified, NZ First leader Winston Peters admitted on Tuesday. However, Peters said the NZ First caucus was satisfied with Morgan's "generous" explanation of his dealings at Aotearoa Television. Page 2.

Troubled Maori television channel Aotearoa Television Network is planning a telethon to raise funds to keep it on air. Staff at the channel have been holding daily meetings to talk over the financial woes of the private company. The channel will go off air unless it can replace the $4 million in government funding that was withdrawn after a row erupted over use of funds. Page 2.

Treasurer Winston Peters angrily rejected yesterday suggestions that his brother Wayne received more than $200,000 of taxpayers' money for his role as a NZ First negotiator during last year's coalition talks. Parliamentary Services general manager John O'Sullivan also cast doubt on the suggestion, saying NZ First had claimed only $122,500 to cover costs of its involvement in the coalition talks. Page 2.

Telecom Corporation has promised a cost-cutting programme, which may mean job cuts, after posting a lower-than-expected December quarter profit of $167.2 million on Tuesday. The profit for the three months to December 31 was down 8.2 percent on the previous quarter. Despite the profit slide, Telecom's share price rose nine cents to end at $6.95 on Tuesday, as the result was apparently better than some gloom merchants had predicted. Page 16.

The Commerce Commission has given the natural gas industry a matter of months to reach a solution on renegotiating 1980 wholesale contract acts otherwise it will seek compliance through the courts. The commission's chief investigator in the network industries unit, David Taylor, told an energy conference in Auckland on Tuesday that the 1980 contracts were anti-competitive and breached the Commerce Act. Page 16.

A fall in property was reflected in Ports of Auckland tax-paid profit of $17.36 million for the six months to December 31, which was 29 percent lower than the corresponding period last year. Chairman Sir Richard Carter said the sale of part land around the Viaduct Basin -- the future home of the Americas Cup -- had come with restructuring of the property division so that the company could focus on port commercial services. Page 16.

More than 20 million tonnes of overseas cargo were loaded and 11.8 million tonnes were unloaded at New Zealand ports in the year to December, Statistics New Zealand said. In all New Zealand ports, overseas cargo valued at $21.55 billion was loaded in the 12-month period and cargo valued at $21.15 billion was unloaded. Page 16.

The landmark Kapuni gas judgement delivered by Justice Sir Ian Barker this month will break Natural Gas Corporation's dominance of wholesale gas supply. Importantly, it has also enabled the public to gain a rare insight into the modus operandi of a monopoly that has for more than 30 years used its dominance for what was shown to be anti-competitive behaviour and pricing. Page 17.
THE NEW ZEALAND HERALD

Labour charged into a new era in New Zealand politics on Tuesday with the suggestion that New Zealand First MP Tukoroirangi Morgan stood to gain from more taxpayer funding to Aotearoa Television. It was the most serious implication in a string of questions and innuendo unleashed against the embattled MP and former Aotearoa Television director under the protection of parliamentary priviledge. The MP for Hutt South, Trevor Mallard, led the charge on the first day in the house of the new MMP Parliament. ----

The New Zealand First leader, Winston Peters, produced documents on Tuesday which he claims prove that Tukoroirangi Morgan was authorised to spend Aotearoa Television money on clothes. The documents are letters from Aotearoa Television to Te Mangai Paho, the Maori broadcasting funding agency. Peters first highlighted a statement last June by the former financial controller Derek Burns. It said an expenditure control system, requiring budget controllers to authorise commitment of funds from their budgets, was being tested and refined.

A crackdown on costs was signalled by the Telecom chief executive, Dr Roderick Deane, on Tuesday as the company reported its weakest quarterly profit for nearly two years. Net earnings of $167.2 million for the December 1996 quarter were at the low end of analysts' expectations.

Ports of Auckland has lifted its interim dividend by one cent a share to nine cents but posted a 29 percent lower tax-paid profit of $17.36 million for the December half-year. The fully imputed dividend will be paid on March 19. Sir Richard Carter, the chairman, said the half-year profit reflected the company discontinuing some activities after the sale of land around the Viaduct Basin last year.

Fletcher Challenge has begun the search for chief executive Hugh Fletcher's successor, engaging an international headhunting firm. Late last year, Fletcher indicated that he would step down from the company his grandfather founded when he turned 50 on November 28.

The Commerce Commission on Tuesday warned that it is prepared to consider court action if barriers to competition within the natural gas industry were not removed soon. The monopolies watchdog expressed concern back in 1993, when the industry was deregulated, at anti-competitive aspects of the Natural Gas Corporation's 1980 wholesale gas supply contracts.

Many people are affronted by disclosure of information about them through public registers for purposes unrelated to the register, says the Privacy Commissioner, Bruce Slane. As people become more aware of privacy rights they found such disclosure unacceptable, he told a marketing conference organised by the Institute for International Research.

Whiteware manufacturer Fisher and Paykel's Australian market share has soared since 1991, with the company now one of the top manufacturers in terms of retailer and consumer perceptions, a survey by leading market researcher and forecaster BIS Shrapnel has found. The survey project manager, Ruth O'Grady, said that Fisher and Paykel was always ranked in the middle-to-top among suppliers.

Stewart Dawson Corner, a prime retail property in inner-city Wellington, has been sold for about $9 million. MFL Mutual Fund, one of the country's largest superannuation funds, has bought the redeveloped property at the corner of Lambton Quay and Willis Street from Lambton Properties.

The New Zealand Salmon Company's 50 percent-owned joint venture in Chile, Aquacultivos, is moving to diversify from its heavy dependence on the Japanese market. Peter Townsend, one of the Christchurch-based company's three directors and a former chief executive, told its annual meeting that the Japanese market was soft for both salmon and salmon trout grown by Aquacultivos. However, the company had the impression that the Japanese were not holding large stocks.

The Reserve Bank is expected to circulate a draft discussion paper in the next few weeks suggesting a policy switch that would place more emphasis on short-term interest rates to signal its monetary policy intentions. The paper will be widely circulated for comment among senior market officials, analysts say, as a step towards possible adoption by the central bank.
